content.text:
## Bottom line

**Negotiate. Don’t accept the first offer, and don’t walk away yet.**

The offer is **credible but not compelling enough to leave a job you like**, particularly because:

- You were not looking.
- Your base salary would decrease.
- The normalized compensation increase is only about **5%**.
- Google’s long-term value depends partly on refresh grants that are explicitly not guaranteed.
- Changing companies carries execution, culture, performance-rating, and reorganization risk.

I would seek approximately:

- **Base:** $255,000–$260,000
- **New-hire RSUs:** $1.3M–$1.4M
- **Sign-on:** $100,000
- **Target bonus:** remains 20%

A realistic satisfactory outcome would be roughly:

- **$250,000–$255,000 base**
- **$1.2M–$1.3M RSUs**
- **$50,000–$100,000 sign-on**

If Google will not get the recurring, annualized package to roughly **$600,000 or more**, I would lean toward staying at Meta, assuming the roles are otherwise equally attractive.

---

## How good is the current offer?

### Annualized comparison

Using the simple four-year average for the Google grant:

| Component | Meta current | Google offer |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240,000 | $235,000 |
| Target/expected bonus | $36,000 | $47,000 |
| Annualized equity | $250,000 | $270,000 |
| **Annualized total** | **$526,000** | **$552,000** |

That is only a **$26,000 annual increase**, or approximately **5%**.

That is not much of a premium for a happy, passive candidate. You would be taking company-switching risk for an increase that can disappear because of:

- Different performance ratings or bonus payouts
- Stock-price movement
- A delayed start or vesting date
- Lower-than-expected refresh grants
- A stronger Meta refresh or compensation adjustment

The offer is also below the approximately **$606,000 median reported for Google L6 product managers in the Bay Area**, although third-party compensation data mixes tenured employees, new hires, refresh grants, and stock appreciation, so it is a benchmark rather than an exact offer target. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

Your $235,000 base is reasonable but not aggressive. It is above the midpoint of the specific $183,000–$271,000 posting range, but leaves $36,000 of room below the listed maximum. A currently posted comparable Google Senior PM position lists $192,000–$278,000 plus a 20% bonus and equity. ([google.com](https://www.google.com/about/careers/applications/jobs/results/112598809917170374-senior-product-manager-generative-ai-google-cloud?company=Google&company=Google+Fiber&company=YouTube&employment_type=FULL_TIME&hl=en_US&jlo=en_US&page=25&q=&sort_by=date))

### The next-12-month comparison is different

You said only approximately $200,000 of Meta RSUs vest in the next 12 months. On that basis:

- **Meta next 12 months:** $240K + $36K + $200K = **$476K**
- **Google, if 25% vests in year one:** $235K + $47K + $270K = **$552K**

So Google would be approximately **$76,000 better over the next year**, before considering any sign-on or bonus proration.

But first confirm the actual Google vesting schedule. Reported Google schedules frequently use **38% / 32% / 20% / 10%**, rather than 25% annually. If your grant follows that schedule, excluding stock movement and refresh grants:

| Google year | Equity vest | Estimated TC |
|---|---:|---:|
| Year 1 | $410,400 | **$692,400** |
| Year 2 | $345,600 | **$627,600** |
| Year 3 | $216,000 | **$498,000** |
| Year 4 | $108,000 | **$390,000** |

The average remains $552,000, but the year-to-year economics are radically different. Levels.fyi currently identifies 38/32/20/10 as Google’s main reported schedule, while also showing several alternate schedules. Your offer documents—not general Google practice—control. ([levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/companies/google/salaries/product-manager/locations/san-francisco-bay-area))

A front-loaded schedule is valuable initially but creates a substantial **year-three/year-four cliff**. Refresh grants are supposed to offset that over time, but you should not value uncertain future refreshes as if they are guaranteed. Google itself describes refresh equity as being determined through annual compensation planning based on role, location, performance, managerial discretion, and compensation review. ([services.google.com](https://services.google.com/fh/files/blogs/pay_equity_info_sheet.pdf))

---

## What I would ask for

### Opening request

Ask for the following package:

> **$260,000 base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $100,000 sign-on bonus.**

That produces annualized target compensation of approximately:

- $260K base
- $52K bonus
- $350K annualized equity
- **$662K recurring annualized TC**
- Plus the one-time $100K sign-on

That is an anchor, not necessarily your expected final outcome. It is within the posted base range, and it gives Google room to move one or more components.

### Your practical target

A strong, reasonable settlement would be:

> **$255,000 base + $1.3M equity + $75,000–$100,000 sign-on**

Annualized recurring TC:

- $255K base
- $51K bonus
- $325K equity
- **$631K annualized TC**

This would be a meaningful—approximately 20%—premium over your current stated $526K package.

### Minimum package that should keep you seriously interested

I would establish something around:

> **$250,000 base + $1.2M equity + at least $50,000 sign-on**

That equals approximately:

- $250K base
- $50K target bonus
- $300K annualized equity
- **$600K annualized recurring TC**
- Plus sign-on

That is about a 14% premium over your current $526K. For someone who is already happy and was recruited rather than actively searching, that feels much more defensible.

This is also consistent with the external L6 benchmark: keeping the current $235K base and $47K bonus would require approximately **$1.295M in four-year equity** to reach the reported $606K L6 median.

---

## How to prioritize the components

### 1. Equity

This is the most important lever because it creates the largest difference.

Ask to move from **$1.08M to $1.4M**. If they respond with $1.2M–$1.3M, that may be a good outcome.

Do not let the recruiter substitute verbal expectations about refreshes for guaranteed new-hire equity. Your decision model should be:

- Guaranteed base
- Target bonus, appropriately discounted
- Written new-hire equity
- Written sign-on
- **Zero or heavily discounted value for future refreshes**

Refreshes are upside—not part of the guaranteed offer.

### 2. Base

Ask for **$260K**. Your current $240K base and the listed maximum of $271K make this easy to justify.

Base is especially valuable because:

- The target bonus is calculated from it.
- Future raises generally build on it.
- It is not exposed to stock performance.
- It continues after the initial grant ends.

Moving base from $235K to $255K also raises the target bonus from $47K to $51K, producing a $24K recurring annual improvement.

### 3. Sign-on

Ask for **$100K**.

The rationale should not just be “I’m walking away from $200K of Meta RSUs,” because Google may correctly point out that you receive substantial Google equity during the same period. Instead, frame it as:

- Compensation for leaving a role you are happy in
- Transition and execution risk
- Potential forfeiture or timing disruption of existing equity
- Bonus and refresh-cycle timing
- The absence of a compelling first-offer premium

A sign-on is also useful if Google says base or equity is constrained.

---

## What to say to the recruiter

You can use this nearly verbatim:

> I’m genuinely excited about the role and the team. At the same time, I want to be transparent that I wasn’t actively looking, I’m happy at Meta, and compensation is an important part of what would make the transition worthwhile.
>
> On an annualized basis, the current package is approximately $552,000, compared with roughly $526,000 in my current package. That’s a relatively small premium for changing companies, particularly given that future refresh grants aren’t guaranteed and my current base is already $240,000.
>
> If Google could bring the package to $260,000 base, $1.4 million in new-hire equity, and a $100,000 sign-on bonus, I would be in a much better position to make the move. I understand there may be constraints among the components, so I’m open to different combinations, but I’m looking for annualized recurring compensation in the low-to-mid $600,000s, along with some first-year transition support.
>
> Could you take that back to the compensation team?

If you are prepared to accept a specific package immediately, a stronger version is:

> If you can get to $255,000 base, $1.3 million in equity, and a $100,000 sign-on, I’d be prepared to sign.

**Only say that if you really will sign.** A conditional commitment can be powerful, but breaking it damages credibility.

---

## Questions to get answered in writing

Before evaluating the final package, ask for:

1. **Exact equity vesting percentages by year**
   - Do not accept merely “over four years.”

2. **Vesting frequency and first vest date**
   - Monthly, quarterly, or another schedule?
   - Is there a one-year cliff?

3. **Grant-date mechanics**
   - When is the number of Alphabet shares determined?
   - What stock-price averaging convention is used?

4. **First-year bonus treatment**
   - Is the bonus prorated?
   - When would your first bonus be paid?
   - Is eligibility affected by your start date?

5. **Refresh timing**
   - Would you be eligible for the first compensation cycle after joining?
   - Is there a minimum employment date for consideration?
   - When would an initial refresh begin vesting?

6. **Performance assumptions**
   - Is 20% genuinely the target at expected performance?
   - What individual/company multipliers apply?

7. **Sign-on repayment terms**
   - Is repayment required if you leave within one or two years?
   - Is it prorated?

Given that it is **October 30, 2026**, start-date and compensation-cycle eligibility could materially affect your first bonus or refresh opportunity. Get exact dates rather than general assurances.

---

## Accept, negotiate, or walk?

### At the current offer

My view: **do not accept immediately.**

It is not a bad offer. In fact, it may be attractive over the next 12–24 months if the equity is front-loaded. But on a normalized basis, it is only a modest increase from a job you already like.

### After negotiation

I would categorize the outcome this way:

- **$625K+ recurring annualized TC, with a sign-on:** Strong offer; seriously consider accepting.
- **$600K–$625K recurring, with $50K+ sign-on:** Reasonable switching premium; accept if the role/team is at least as attractive as Meta.
- **$575K–$600K:** Borderline; compensation alone does not clearly justify leaving.
- **Below $575K, with no sign-on:** Stay at Meta unless the Google role has substantially better scope, trajectory, leadership, or personal fit.

### Final recommendation

**Negotiate toward $260K / $1.4M / $100K, aim to land around $255K / $1.3M / $75K–$100K, and treat approximately $600K recurring annualized compensation as your minimum serious switching threshold.**

If Google remains at the current package, I would probably stay at Meta—not because Google’s offer is poor, but because it is not sufficiently better to compensate a happy, high-performing incumbent for taking a voluntary career risk.

content.text:
## My recommendation: **probably take it—if you like the role and manager**

Financially, the revised offer has crossed from “not enough to justify moving” to **a reasonable switching package**.

I would **not negotiate again** after they explicitly called it their best offer. Instead, verify the contractual details, then decide based on the job itself.

## The economics

Assuming the $1.08M grant is valued evenly over four years:

| Component | Meta | Google |
|---|---:|---:|
| Base | $240K | $240K |
| Bonus | $36K | $48K |
| Annualized initial equity | $250K | $270K |
| **Recurring annualized TC** | **$526K** | **$558K** |
| Sign-on | — | **$200K** |

Google’s recurring package is only **$32K higher**, or about **6%**. But spreading the sign-on across four years makes Google’s effective four-year average:

- Google: **$608K/year**
- Meta: **$526K/year**
- Difference: **$82K/year**, or approximately **15.6%**

If Meta compensation stayed at its current run rate, the four-year comparison would be:

- **Google:** $2.432M
- **Meta:** $2.104M
- **Google advantage:** approximately **$328K**

That excludes stock-price changes and uncertain future refreshes at both companies.

## Don’t subtract the $200K twice

It would be a mistake to view the sign-on as merely canceling out the $200K of Meta RSUs you are forfeiting.

If you stay, your stated next-12-month Meta compensation is:

- $240K base
- $36K bonus
- $200K vesting equity
- **Total: $476K**

If Google equity vested evenly and the entire sign-on were paid during the first year:

- $240K base
- $48K target bonus
- $270K Google equity
- $200K sign-on
- **Total: $758K**

That is a nominal **$282K first-year advantage** for Google, before bonus proration, stock movement, vesting timing, and any clawback.

The Google equity is already replacing the equity you leave behind. The sign-on is additional compensation for making the move.

## The important limitation

This is an attractive **four-year offer**, but not necessarily a dramatic long-term raise.

Without the sign-on, Google is only about 6% ahead. After the initial equity grant runs its course, the outcome depends heavily on:

- Google refresh grants
- Your performance rating
- Alphabet stock performance
- Meta compensation and refreshes you would otherwise have received
- Whether you remain at Google long enough to collect the full grant

Therefore, I would characterize the offer as:

- **Very strong in the first year**
- **Solid over four years**
- **Only modestly better on recurring guaranteed/run-rate compensation**

That is enough to accept if the role is genuinely attractive. It is not enough to accept a substantially worse manager, scope, commute, culture, or promotion trajectory.

## Verify these terms before signing

Ask for written confirmation of:

1. **Exact RSU vesting schedule**
   - Percent vesting in each of the four years
   - First vest date
   - Monthly or quarterly vesting
   - Any initial cliff

2. **Sign-on payment date**
   - First paycheck?
   - After 30 or 60 days?
   - Split across two years?

3. **Sign-on repayment obligation**
   - How long is the clawback period?
   - Is repayment prorated monthly?
   - Does repayment apply if Google terminates you without cause?
   - Does it apply after a reorganization or role elimination?

   A 12-month prorated clawback is manageable. A two-year, non-prorated clawback materially reduces the offer’s attractiveness.

4. **Bonus proration**
   - Since today is **October 30, 2026**, your start date may materially affect your first bonus.
   - Confirm exactly when you become eligible and what your first target payout would be.

5. **Equity grant mechanics**
   - When is the share count established?
   - What price or averaging period is used?
   - Is the stated $1.08M subject to final board approval?

6. **Refresh eligibility**
   - When are you first eligible for consideration?
   - Could your start date cause you to miss an annual compensation cycle?

Do not confuse withholding with final tax liability: bonuses may initially have federal income tax withheld using supplemental-wage rules, but your ultimate tax is determined through your full tax return. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15?utm_source=openai))

## Decision rule

### I would accept if:

- You believe the Google role and manager are at least reasonably comparable to Meta.
- The scope offers credible growth or stronger career optionality.
- The $200K sign-on is paid promptly.
- The clawback is reasonable.
- The vesting schedule does not contain an unfavorable surprise.
- You can tolerate the possibility that refresh grants are smaller than expected.

### I would stay at Meta if:

- You clearly prefer your Meta manager, product area, or scope.
- You are close to promotion or a significant refresh.
- The Google role has vague ownership or questionable organizational stability.
- The sign-on has harsh repayment terms.
- You are considering Google almost entirely because the $200K headline feels large.

## Bottom line

**On compensation alone, I would take the revised offer.** Google has preserved the original equity, matched your base, increased your target bonus, and added a full $200K sign-on. That produces a meaningful four-year switching premium.

But the offer is not so overwhelming that you should ignore job quality. My final decision would be:

> **Accept if the Google role and manager are at least 80–90% as attractive as your current situation. Stay if you materially prefer the actual work and leadership at Meta.**

At this point, the decision is no longer “Did Google pay enough?” They probably did. The decision is whether the role itself is good enough to justify leaving a situation where you are already happy.
